title: Party Drinking Tips: How to Pace Yourself and Stay Safe
excerpt: Practical tips for drinking at a party: what to eat first, how to pace yourself, how to say no, how to handle shots and drinking games, and the signs a friend needs help.
metaDescription: Drinking at a party? How to pace yourself, what to eat first, how to turn down drinks, and the alcohol poisoning signs that mean you should call for help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The short answer:** the best party drinking plan is simple. Eat a real meal before you go, decide on a rough drink limit before the first sip, alternate every alcoholic drink with water or something non-alcoholic, and aim for about one standard drink per hour or less. Those four habits do more for how you feel at the party, how you get home, and how you feel the next morning than any trick, pill, or drink order. The rest of this guide explains why each one works, how to stick to them when everyone around you is drinking faster, and how to spot the point where a friend needs real help.

**The quick rules:** Eat first. Know what a standard drink looks like. Pace yourself to roughly one drink an hour. Alternate with water. Skip drinking games and shots if you want to stay in control. Keep your drink in your hand. Plan your ride home before you leave the house. And if someone can't be woken up, is breathing slowly, or is vomiting while barely conscious, call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away.

> **This is not medical advice.** This guide is general information for adults of legal drinking age who choose to drink socially. It isn't a substitute for advice from a doctor who knows your health. **Talk to a doctor before drinking if** you take prescription medicines (especially sedatives, sleep aids, anxiety medicines, opioids, or antihistamines), are pregnant or trying to get pregnant, have liver, heart, or stomach problems, or have been told to avoid alcohol. **Call 911 or your local emergency number** if someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning: they can't be woken, they're confused or having a seizure, they're breathing slowly or irregularly, their skin is pale, bluish, or cold, or they're vomiting while drowsy or unconscious.

## Why Parties Are Harder to Drink Sensibly At Than a Normal Night Out

At a bar or a dinner, you usually order one drink at a time, the drinks come in fixed sizes, and someone brings you a bill. Parties remove nearly every one of those natural brakes. That's why so many people say they "didn't drink that much" at a party and still felt terrible the next day.

Here's what changes:

- **Pours are bigger and uneven.** Home pours of wine and spirits are almost always bigger than a bar's standard measure. A red cup of "vodka soda" mixed by a friend can easily hold two or three standard drinks.
- **Refills happen without you asking.** A host topping up your glass means you lose count, because you never actually finish a drink.
- **There's no clock.** Without last orders, closing time, or a bill, a party can run for six hours, and drinks spread across that much time add up.
- **The food is unpredictable.** Snacks may run out early, or the "food" may be chips and dip rather than a meal.
- **Group pressure is stronger.** Rounds of shots, drinking games, and "one more" from friends are harder to turn down in a living room than at a bar.

None of this means you can't enjoy a party. It means the plan needs to be made *before* you get there, because the setting is designed to make you forget it.

## Know What a Standard Drink Actually Is

You can't pace yourself if you don't know what you're counting. In the United States, a "standard drink" contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol. According to the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), that's roughly:

| Drink | Standard drink size | Typical party reality |
|---|---|---|
| Regular beer (about 5% ABV) | 12 oz (one can) | Craft IPAs at 7 to 9% can be 1.5 to 2 drinks per can |
| Wine (about 12% ABV) | 5 oz | A generous home pour is often 7 to 9 oz, closer to 1.5 to 2 drinks |
| Spirits (40% ABV, 80 proof) | 1.5 oz (one shot) | Free-poured mixed drinks often contain 2 to 3 oz of liquor |
| Hard seltzer (about 5% ABV) | 12 oz | Some "high-ABV" seltzers run 8% or more |
| Punch or "jungle juice" | Impossible to know | Often much stronger than it tastes |

Two practical takeaways. First, check the ABV printed on cans before you open them, because the difference between a 4.5% light beer and an 8% double IPA is nearly double the alcohol. Second, be very careful with mystery punch. Sugary mixers hide the taste of alcohol, and you have no idea how much was poured in. For a full breakdown by drink type, see our guide to [alcohol content by drink](/never-hungover/alcohol-content-by-drink).

## Before the Party: Set Yourself Up

Most of what decides how the night goes happens in the hour before you leave.

### Eat a proper meal

This is the single most useful thing you can do. Food in your stomach slows the rate at which alcohol moves into your small intestine, which is where most of it gets absorbed. Slower absorption means a lower peak blood alcohol level from the same number of drinks, which means you feel more in control and are less likely to get sick.

The best pre-party meal includes protein, some fat, and fiber-rich carbohydrates: think a chicken or bean burrito bowl, salmon with rice and vegetables, eggs on toast with avocado, or pasta with a meat or lentil sauce. A light snack is better than nothing, but a full meal works better. Our guides to [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) and [why drinking on an empty stomach hits so hard](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) go into more detail.

### Hydrate, but don't overdo it

Show up well hydrated by drinking normally through the day and having a glass or two of water with your meal. You don't need to chug a liter before you leave; that just sends you looking for the bathroom.

### Decide your limit in advance

Pick a number before you arrive, while you're thinking clearly. It doesn't have to be strict, but having one changes how you drink. "Three drinks over the evening" is a plan. "I'll see how I feel" usually becomes six. A useful benchmark: US dietary guidelines describe moderate drinking as up to two drinks a day for men and up to one for women, and the NIAAA defines binge drinking as about five or more drinks for men or four or more for women within roughly two hours.

### Plan your ride home now

Decide how you're getting home before you have your first drink. Book the designated driver, check that your rideshare app works, save a taxi number, or arrange to stay over. The decision you make sober is always better than the one you make at 1 a.m.

### Check your medications

If you take anything regularly, especially sleep aids, anxiety medication, antidepressants, painkillers, antihistamines, or diabetes medicine, check the label or ask a pharmacist whether it interacts with alcohol. Some combinations make you far more sedated than you expect from the number of drinks.

### Charge your phone

It sounds trivial, but a dead phone is how people end up stranded, separated from friends, or unable to call for help. Leave the house with a full battery.

## At the Party: How to Pace Yourself

Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady rate, roughly one standard drink per hour for an average adult, though this varies a lot with body size, sex, genetics, and other factors. You can't speed it up with coffee, cold showers, or exercise. That's why pacing matters: if you drink faster than your liver can keep up, the extra alcohol builds up in your blood.

### The one-drink-an-hour rule

Aim for no more than about one standard drink per hour. Over a four-hour party, that's four drinks spread out, not four in the first hour followed by a long, sloppy evening. If you want to see roughly how different drinking speeds affect blood alcohol, our [blood alcohol calculator](/never-hungover/blood-alcohol-calculator) gives a rough estimate (it's a guide, not a sobriety test).

### Alternate every drink with water

Have a glass of water, soda water, or a non-alcoholic drink between each alcoholic one. This does three things: it slows your pace without you having to think about it, it gives your hands something to hold so people stop offering you refills, and it keeps you somewhat hydrated. Alcohol suppresses a hormone (vasopressin) that normally helps your kidneys hold on to water, so you lose more fluid than usual while drinking. Some people call alternating "zebra striping"; we cover the idea in our piece on the [zebra striping trend](/never-hungover/zebra-striping-drinking-trend-2025).

Water won't prevent a hangover by itself, since dehydration is only one part of what causes one. Hangovers also involve inflammation, poor sleep, and the by-products of breaking down alcohol, which water doesn't touch.

### Finish your drink before taking another

Don't let anyone top up a half-full glass. Finish it, then decide whether you want another. This simple rule keeps your count honest.

### Sip, don't gulp

Choose drinks you enjoy slowly. A glass of wine or a beer is easier to make last than a sweet mixed drink you barely taste.

### Keep eating through the night

Graze on whatever food is available, especially anything with protein or fat. If the snacks are thin, step out for food or eat a little more before you go next time.

### Watch the bubbles

Some small studies suggest that alcohol mixed with carbonated mixers, such as champagne or spirits with soda, may be absorbed somewhat faster than the same drink without bubbles. The evidence isn't strong, but it's one more reason to sip sparkling drinks slowly rather than toss them back.

## Shots, Drinking Games, and Pre-Gaming: The Biggest Risks

If you want one rule for staying in control at a party, it's this: the dangerous drinking happens fast. Shots, drinking games, and pre-gaming all share the same problem. They push a lot of alcohol into your body in a short time, before you feel its full effect.

### Why shots hit harder than you expect

A shot gets swallowed in seconds. Your blood alcohol keeps rising for 30 to 90 minutes after you stop drinking as the alcohol is absorbed. So three shots in 20 minutes can feel fine at first, then land all at once. That delay is why people often say "I was fine, and then suddenly I wasn't."

### Drinking games

Beer pong, flip cup, and "never have I ever" are fun, but they take the decision about when to drink away from you. If you play, you can:

- Use water or a lighter beer in your cups
- Play a round or two, then sit out
- Take the role of scorekeeper or referee
- Agree with friends before the game starts that losing means a sip, not a full cup

### Pre-gaming

Drinking at home before heading out is common because it's cheaper, but it's also where many people blow their limit before the party even starts. If you pre-game, count those drinks as part of your night, not as a separate event. Our [pre-game party strategy guide](/never-hungover/pre-game-party-strategy-dhm-2025) covers how to approach the hours before a big night.

## Does Mixing Drinks Make It Worse?

You'll hear "beer before liquor, never been sicker" at almost every party. The research doesn't support the idea that the *order* of drinks matters. A 2019 study published in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* tested beer-then-wine against wine-then-beer and found that the order made no meaningful difference to hangover severity. What mattered was how much people drank and how drunk they got. We explain the study in [the beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth).

What *is* true:

- **Switching drinks often makes you lose count.** Moving from beer to cocktails to shots makes it harder to keep track of how much you've had.
- **Darker drinks may make hangovers a little worse for some people.** Drinks like bourbon, brandy, and red wine contain more congeners, by-products of fermentation and aging. A study by researchers at Brown University found bourbon produced somewhat worse hangovers than vodka at the same blood alcohol level. Clear drinks aren't hangover-proof, though.
- **Sugary mixers mask strength.** Sweet cocktails and punch go down easily, which makes them easy to drink fast.

## How to Say No (or "Not Yet") Without Making It a Thing

Most of the pressure at parties is friendly, not hostile. People offer drinks because they want you to have a good time. A few easy ways to handle it:

- **Keep a drink in your hand.** A full glass of anything, including soda water with lime, means people stop offering.
- **Use a simple, final answer.** "I'm good for now, thanks" or "I'm pacing myself tonight" works. You don't owe anyone a longer explanation.
- **Give a practical reason if you want one.** "I'm driving," "Early start tomorrow," or "I've got a workout in the morning" usually ends the conversation.
- **Bring your own non-alcoholic option.** A few cans of non-alcoholic beer or sparkling water mean you always have something to reach for. If you're curious how much alcohol non-alcoholic beer really contains, see [does non-alcoholic beer have alcohol](/never-hungover/does-non-alcoholic-beer-have-alcohol).
- **Make the shot a "cheers" instead.** Raise your glass for the toast, then sip.

If a friend keeps pushing after you've said no, that's their problem, not yours. A good friend will back off.

## Stay Safe: Your Drink, Your Friends, Your Way Home

### Look after your drink

Drink spiking is less common than its reputation suggests, but it does happen, and alcohol itself is the substance most often used to impair someone. Practical habits:

- Pour or open your own drinks when you can
- Keep your drink in your hand or in sight
- Don't drink from a glass you put down and walked away from; get a fresh one
- Be wary of shared punch bowls at parties where you don't know people

If you or a friend suddenly feel much drunker than the number of drinks would explain, feel confused, or are struggling to stay awake or move, get to a safe place with someone you trust and get medical help.

### Use the buddy system

Arrive with a friend and agree to leave together, or at least check in before anyone heads home. Don't let a drunk friend walk home alone or go off with someone they just met when they're clearly impaired.

### Getting home

Never drive after drinking, and never get in a car with a driver who has been drinking. You can be impaired well before you feel drunk. Use the plan you made before the party: a designated driver, rideshare, taxi, public transit, or a couch.

## When a Friend Needs Help: Alcohol Poisoning Signs

This is the most important section in this guide. Alcohol poisoning happens when blood alcohol rises so high that it starts shutting down the parts of the brain that control breathing, heart rate, and body temperature. It's a medical emergency, and it's most likely after fast drinking, especially shots and drinking games.

> **Call 911 or your local emergency number right away if someone:**
> - Can't be woken up, or is very hard to wake
> - Is confused, or is having a seizure
> - Is vomiting while drowsy, passed out, or barely responsive
> - Is breathing slowly (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute) or irregularly, with long pauses
> - Has pale, bluish, or cold, clammy skin
>
> They don't need to have every sign. One is enough to call.

While you wait for help:

- **Don't leave them alone.** Their condition can get worse even after they stop drinking, because alcohol in their stomach is still being absorbed.
- **Roll them onto their side** (the recovery position) so they won't choke if they vomit.
- **Keep them warm** with a blanket or jacket.
- **Don't give them coffee, a cold shower, or anything to "sober them up."** None of these work, and a cold shower can make low body temperature worse.
- **Don't let them "sleep it off"** if they show any of the signs above.
- **Tell the paramedics what they drank** and whether they took any medicines or drugs.

Many people hesitate to call because they're worried about getting a friend (or themselves) in trouble. Many US states and many universities have medical amnesty or Good Samaritan policies that protect people who call for help in an alcohol emergency; check the rules where you live. Either way, calling is always the right choice. For more detail, read our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs).

## When You Get Home

The last hour of the night has a big effect on the next morning.

- **Drink a glass or two of water** before bed. Keep another next to the bed.
- **Eat something small** if you're hungry, like toast, crackers, or a banana.
- **Skip the extra "nightcap."** Alcohol may help you fall asleep faster, but it disrupts sleep in the second half of the night, which is a big reason you feel wrecked the next day.
- **Don't take Tylenol "just in case" before bed.** Acetaminophen and alcohol both put work on your liver. If you wake up with a headache, deal with it then, after eating. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why.
- **Don't take sleep aids.** Alcohol plus a sedating sleep aid can slow your breathing more than either one alone.
- **If you've had a lot to drink, sleep on your side** and, if you're staying with friends, let someone know.

## The Next Morning

If you followed the plan, you'll probably wake up feeling reasonable. If you didn't, here's what helps:

- **Rehydrate steadily.** Water is the basic option. If you vomited or sweated a lot, an electrolyte drink can help replace salts; see our comparison of [the best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks).
- **Eat a real breakfast.** Eggs, toast, fruit, and something salty usually go down well.
- **Rest.** Time is the only thing that fully clears a hangover. Most hangovers fade within 24 hours.
- **Go easy on painkillers.** If you take one, take a single label dose with food, and don't stack products.
- **Skip "hair of the dog."** Another drink only delays the hangover.

Our main guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the evidence behind each step.

### When a hangover is more than a hangover

A normal hangover is miserable but gets steadily better through the day. See a doctor if you have vomiting that won't stop or you can't keep fluids down, vomit that contains blood or looks like coffee grounds, severe stomach pain, chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle, confusion, or symptoms that are getting worse rather than better after a day. If you notice shaking, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart that shows up when you *haven't* been drinking and eases when you drink, tell a doctor plainly; that can be a sign of physical dependence and is worth getting checked.

## Party Situations: Quick Playbooks

### House party with friends

Eat first, bring your own drinks so you know their strength, and alternate with water. Offer to help the host, which keeps you busy and away from the shot table.

### Office party or work event

Treat it as a work event with drinks, not a night out. Two drinks is a sensible ceiling for most people. Eat early, and leave before the crowd gets loud. For seasonal events, see our [holiday drinking survival guide](/never-hungover/holiday-drinking-survival-guide-health-first-approach).

### Wedding or all-day celebration

These can last eight hours or more, often with champagne toasts, an open bar, and late food. Eat breakfast and lunch, skip drinks during the gap between ceremony and reception, and keep a water glass with you all night. Champagne goes down easily, so sip the toasts.

### College or big crowded party

This is where drinking games, mystery punch, and spiked drinks are most common. Stick with friends, pour your own drinks or open sealed cans, avoid the punch, and agree in advance who's watching out for whom.

### Hosting the party

Serve real food, not just snacks, and keep it coming. Put out water and good non-alcoholic options in plain sight. Use a jigger or measuring cup for mixed drinks. Stop serving alcohol an hour or so before the party ends, and make sure everyone has a safe ride home.

## What About Hangover Supplements?

No supplement makes it safe to drink fast, drive after drinking, or ignore the signs above. Pacing, food, and water are what actually protect you on the night.

That said, some people add a supplement as one small part of their routine. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, is the one we cover most on this site. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so think of it as promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own or lowers your blood alcohol, and it does not make you safer to drive. If you want to try it alongside the habits above, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- Eat a real meal before you go, and keep eating through the night.
- Know what a standard drink looks like, and remember home pours are bigger.
- Decide your limit before you arrive, and aim for about one drink an hour or less.
- Alternate every alcoholic drink with water or a non-alcoholic option.
- Be most careful with shots, drinking games, pre-gaming, and mystery punch.
- Keep your drink in sight, stick with friends, and plan your way home before the first drink.
- If someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly, or is vomiting while barely conscious, call 911 right away.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How do you pace yourself drinking at a party?**

Aim for about one standard drink per hour or less, which is roughly the rate an average adult's liver clears alcohol. Alternate every alcoholic drink with a glass of water or a non-alcoholic drink, finish each drink before accepting a refill, and decide on a rough limit before you arrive. Eating a real meal beforehand slows absorption and makes pacing easier.

**What should I eat before drinking at a party?**

A full meal with protein, some fat, and fiber-rich carbohydrates works best, such as a burrito bowl, salmon with rice, eggs on toast with avocado, or pasta with a meat or lentil sauce. Food slows how fast alcohol moves into your small intestine, which lowers your peak blood alcohol level from the same number of drinks. A small snack is better than nothing, but a meal works better.

**How many drinks is too many at a party?**

There's no single safe number for everyone. As a benchmark, US dietary guidelines describe moderate drinking as up to two drinks a day for men and one for women, and the NIAAA defines binge drinking as about five or more drinks for men or four or more for women in roughly two hours. Remember that home pours are often bigger than a standard drink, so three cups at a party can be more than three drinks.

**Does drinking water between drinks help?**

Yes, mainly because it slows your pace and keeps you a bit more hydrated. Alcohol makes your kidneys release more water than usual, so alternating helps offset some of that loss. Water alone won't prevent a hangover, though, because dehydration is only one part of what causes one.

**Does mixing drinks make you more drunk or more hungover?**

The order of drinks doesn't matter much. A 2019 study in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition found beer-then-wine and wine-then-beer produced similar hangovers. What matters is how much you drink and how fast. Switching drinks does make it easier to lose count, and darker drinks like bourbon and red wine may cause somewhat worse hangovers for some people.

**How do I turn down drinks at a party without it being awkward?**

Keep a drink in your hand (soda water with lime works), give a short answer like "I'm good for now, thanks," or offer a practical reason such as driving or an early start. Bringing your own non-alcoholic drinks also helps. You don't owe anyone a long explanation.

**What are the signs a friend has alcohol poisoning?**

Call 911 or your local emergency number if someone can't be woken or is very hard to wake, is confused or having a seizure, is vomiting while drowsy or unconscious, is breathing slowly or irregularly, or has pale, bluish, or cold skin. Stay with them, roll them onto their side, keep them warm, and don't let them sleep it off. One sign is enough to call.

**Can a supplement let me drink more at a party?**

No. No supplement makes it safe to drink fast or drive after drinking, and none lowers your blood alcohol in a way you can rely on. Some people take DHM as part of their routine, but its research is mostly from animal and lab studies with limited human data, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own. Pacing, food, and water are what protect you on the night.
